tagline: Logging routes became a mountain drive past waterfalls and a forestry school
intro: Forest Heritage Scenic Byway climbs through Pisgah National Forest on roads with steep grades, quick turns and a switchback descent into the Pink Beds. The state-designated route follows NC 215 and US 276 for 64.4 miles. North Carolina’s transportation department presents the drive as a way to explore forestlands, waterfalls and mountain views, and gives a driving time of one hour and 50 minutes.

Much of the road occupies former logging railroad routes used in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The Forest Service established the byway in 1989, followed by state designation in 1990. In 2009, part of US 276 received National Scenic Byway designation, a shorter section within this broader drive. The separate National Forest Scenic Byway adds US 64 to complete a loop; the state route ends without that return leg.

Starting near Rosman, follow NC 215 beside the North Fork French Broad River through Balsam Grove and up to Beech Gap. Descend to Lake Logan, then turn onto US 276 at Woodrow and climb beside the East Fork Pigeon River. Beyond Wagon Road Gap come the Pink Beds, Cradle of Forestry, Sliding Rock and Looking Glass Falls, before the state byway ends at US 64 and NC 280 near Brevard.

moments.title: Cradle of Forestry
moments.text: At the Cradle of Forestry, a logging locomotive and a portable sawmill belong to the story of a school. Carl A. Schenck taught forestry on George Vanderbilt’s estate, combining classroom work with practical training in the woods. Students learned to fell trees, operate machinery, transplant seedlings and tend nurseries. Their summer lodgings at Pink Beds carried names including Hell Hole, Little Bohemia and The Palace. The school closed in 1913. Its grounds now form a historic site with exhibits on forestry and forest conservation. Two trails include original school buildings as well as the machinery used to interpret this working forest history.

moments.title: Sliding Rock
moments.text: Looking Glass Creek takes a gentler route here, spreading down a sloping rock face into a deep pool. Sliding Rock is about 60 feet long, and its name describes the way visitors ride the waterfall into the water below. Locals and tourists have long used the rock as a natural waterslide; the Forest Service developed the site as a recreation area. A viewing platform provides another way to take in the falls. The lower platform was destroyed in flooding in the summer of 2021. The water stays near 55 degrees Fahrenheit year round, even when summer draws people to the slide.

moments.title: Looking Glass Falls
moments.text: Looking Glass Falls puts a 60-foot waterfall beside the byway, with a pull-off for viewing it. Looking Glass Creek flows through Pisgah National Forest and supplies the falls. The name also points to nearby Looking Glass Rock, whose granite face reflects sunlight. Water seeping across that stone creates the mirrorlike effect described by North Carolina’s transportation department. The rock and waterfall share a name, but the roadside stop is the falls, directly beside US 276. In winter, water freezing on the rock’s sides reflects sunlight, another expression of the mirror that gave the rock its name.
moments.notice: Notice the 60-foot drop beside the road.
